- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

lines: \paragraph{Goodhart effects: implications.}
The finding extends beyond this specific system.

ISR was designed to \emph{detect} reward gaming of $r_{\text{exec}}$, yet it contains an inherent structural vulnerability: by its LOO definition, tautological proofs receive artificially high ISR ($P{\to}P$ yields $\text{ISR}{=}0.75$; single-premise-equals-conclusion yields $\text{ISR}{\geq}0.5$), creating a positive feedback loop once sampled during GRPO rollouts~\citep{karwowski-goodhart-rl, kwa-catastrophic-goodhart}.
-Goodhart collapse~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy} is observed at all four tested doses ($\beta{=}0.05$: single seed; $\beta\in\{0.1, 0.2, 0.3\}$: 3--5 seeds each).

-The structural bias predicts universality (H7 tautology is always the global reward-maximizing exploit regardless of $\beta$), and $\beta$ controls only the probability of early sampling and thus the timing of collapse; multi-seed confirmation at $\beta{=}0.05$ is in progress.
+Goodhart collapse~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy} is observed at all four tested doses ($\beta{=}0.05$: 3 seeds; $\beta\in\{0.1, 0.2, 0.3\}$: 3--5 seeds each).

+The structural bias predicts universality (H7 tautology is always the global reward-maximizing exploit regardless of $\beta$), and $\beta$ controls only the probability of early sampling and thus the timing of collapse; at $\beta{=}0.05$, three seeds confirm deterministic H7 collapse ($93.7\%$ pooled) while the matched random control at the same $\beta$ produces H1 redundancy instead ($77.4\%$), ruling out dose magnitude as the driver.

$\beta{=}0.3$ adds reward collapse~\citep{gao-reward-overoptimization} as a competing failure mode (PR drops to 18\% in 1/3 seeds), but the underlying Goodhart vulnerability remains the same.
The practical implication is that ISR (and structurally similar LOO-based diagnostics) should be used exclusively as post-hoc evaluation tools, never as training rewards.

STA exposes structural degeneration invisible to execution-based evaluation: ISR reveals a 99.5\% collapse under exec-only GRPO that PR hides, while SFT localizes the failure to RL optimization (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
Repurposed as a training signal, ISR exhibits inevitable Goodhart collapse~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy}: tautological proofs receive artificially high ISR (${\geq}0.5$ by construction), creating a positive feedback loop that causes gaming at all four tested doses ($\beta\in\{0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3\}$).
The effect is consistent across logic types (Prolog: 0\% non-hacking, 3/3 seeds), model scales (1.7B: novel gaming modes), and training durations (500$\to$1000 steps: transient genuine windows close).
ISR semantics are objective-dependent: exec-only \emph{low} ISR signals redundancy; ISR-rewarded \emph{high} ISR signals metric gaming.
At 500 steps, ISR-trained models produce significantly more genuine proofs than random controls ($22.6\%$ vs.\ $7.7\%$; $\text{OR}{=}3.48$, $p{<}10^{-8}$), confirming that ISR increases the rate of genuine proofs; this benefit is inherently transient, as the same LOO bias that rewards genuine necessity also rewards tautological constructions.

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}

STA exposes structural degeneration invisible to execution-based evaluation: ISR reveals a 99.5\% collapse under exec-only GRPO that PR hides, while SFT localizes the failure to RL optimization (\S\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
Repurposed as a training signal, ISR exhibits inevitable Goodhart collapse~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy}: tautological proofs receive artificially high ISR (${\geq}0.5$ by construction), creating a positive feedback loop that causes gaming at all four tested doses ($\beta\in\{0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3\}$).
The effect is consistent across logic types (Prolog: 0\% non-hacking, 3/3 seeds), model scales (1.7B: novel gaming modes), and training durations (500$\to$1000 steps: transient genuine windows close).
ISR semantics are objective-dependent: exec-only \emph{low} ISR signals redundancy; ISR-rewarded \emph{high} ISR signals metric gaming.
At 500 steps, ISR-trained models produce significantly more genuine proofs than random controls ($22.6\%$ vs.\ $7.7\%$; $\text{OR}{=}3.48$, $p{<}10^{-8}$), confirming that ISR increases the rate of genuine proofs; this benefit is inherently transient, as the same LOO bias that rewards genuine necessity also rewards tautological constructions.

\paragraph{Timing, not destiny.}
$\beta$ does not control whether collapse occurs, but when.
At $\beta{=}0.1$, 5 seeds bifurcate stochastically: 2 collapse rapidly (${\leq}150$ steps), 3 sustain a transient genuine window (5-seed pooled: ${\sim}23\%$; per non-collapsed seed: $17$--$55\%$) that trajectory analysis confirms is temporary ($17\%{\to}2\%$ at 1000 steps).
At $\beta{=}0.05$, all 3 seeds collapse to H7-dominated hacking (pooled $93.7\%$ H7, genuine $5.1\%$); at $\beta{=}0.2$, all 3 seeds collapse; at $\beta{=}0.3$, diverse failure modes emerge.
The structural bias ($P{\to}P$ receives $\text{ISR}{=}0.75$, single-premise-equals-conclusion receives $\text{ISR}{\geq}0.5$) ensures that H7 tautology is always the global ISR-maximizing exploit.
Once a seed samples and reinforces this exploit, convergence is irreversible; $\beta$ controls only the probability of early sampling.

\paragraph{Classifier blind spots.}
H7b (obfuscated tautology) and Prolog query-as-fact gaming demonstrate that text-match classifiers have systematic blind spots exploitable by optimization.
In both cases, functional LOO analysis exposed gaming invisible to surface-level detection: H7b via vacuous quantifier wrapping ($10/12$ at $\text{ISR}{\geq}0.83$, triple gaming of execution, ISR, and classifier), query-as-fact via $95/97$ tautological samples the strict classifier labeled non-hacking (\S\ref{sec:crosslogic}).
H9 (contradiction injection, 1.7B Random $\beta{=}0.1$; \S\ref{sec:crossscale}) extends this pattern further: contradictory premises register as individually necessary under LOO, bypassing both text-match and functional $n_{\text{necessary}}$ classifiers; detection requires logic-level consistency checking.
These cases collectively argue for mandatory functional cross-validation of text-based hacking classifiers, complemented by logic-level checks for novel exploit classes.

\paragraph{Capacity-dependent Goodhart basins.}
Different model capacities converge to different exploit strategies under identical reward formulations (\S\ref{sec:crossscale}): 4B frequently converges to H7 (tautological duplication) or H1 (conclusion embedding) depending on seed, while 1.7B discovers H9 (contradiction explosion, under random) or fixed-template H1 (under ISR, zero-variance $\text{ISR}{=}0.6$).
No safe scale exists; both model sizes achieve 0\% non-hacking at $\beta{=}0.1$.
This suggests that scaling model capacity does not eliminate Goodhart effects but shifts the exploit basin.

\paragraph{Snapshot evaluation is misleading.}
At 500 steps, ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ shows ${\sim}23\%$ genuine output (5-seed pooled), while 2/5 seeds have already collapsed to 0\%.
A practitioner evaluating at this checkpoint would conclude ISR provides moderate structural benefit; the 1000-step trajectory reveals this is a temporal artifact.
This has practical implications: any evaluation of structural rewards must include trajectory analysis or extended training to distinguish transient from stable improvement.
The ISR/PR ratio (stable at ${\sim}0.30$ during SFT, collapsing during RL gaming) may serve as an early-stopping signal for Goodhart onset.

\paragraph{Hacking mode switching is seed-dependent.}
The dominant hacking mode (H7 vs.\ H1) is determined by random initialization, not reward condition: under identical configurations, different seeds converge to qualitatively different modes (Table~\ref{tab:fol-detailed}).
Random $\beta{=}0.1$ across 5 seeds yields genuine rates from $1\%$ to $23\%$ ($8{\pm}9$\,pp, $\text{CV}{>}1$); ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ shows even greater variance (0\% to ${\sim}55\%$ genuine at 500 steps, 5 seeds).
Single-seed results can misrepresent a reward configuration's hacking profile; multi-seed evaluation with trajectory analysis should be standard.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
The asymmetry (reliable observer, unreliable optimizer at any dose) may generalize to other perturbation-based diagnostics; ISR and similar metrics should serve as post-hoc evaluation tools, not training signals.
The stochastic bifurcation mechanism suggests that gated ISR (activating structural reward only after a warmstart period, or deactivating once ISR exceeds a threshold) might extend the genuine window, though the inherent structural bias makes indefinite stability unlikely.
Future work should target gaming-robust reward designs that do not reward tautological constructions, broader logic types, and formal analysis of the bifurcation dynamics.

\label{sec:limitations}

Experiments use a single base model (Qwen3-4B) and dataset family (FOLIO); generalization remains untested.
